persons.name: Kaelyn (catfished by friend)
persons.harm: From about age 19, a friend catfished her for years through invented personas (a harasser 'Lexi', a love interest 'Tyler' who supposedly killed himself, and his 'sister' who would sell her a car), leaving her with years of guilt over the fake suicide; the friend also pressed her to send money for the car before she had it.
persons.perpetrator_role: a female friend she met by text (catfisher)
persons.outcome_quote: No, I don't know if she just deleted her whole account or if she just deleted me, but I saw that we're not friends on Facebook anymore
persons.notes: No institution (police, platform, employer) is mentioned at any point. She exposed the catfishing herself (contacting the perpetrator's ex-husband) and later via a viral TikTok video (6.5 million views); the perpetrator appeared on MTV's Catfish (as the person catfished). Neither the TikTok nor the TV show is an institution with a duty to respond, so not coded as contacts. The never-reached quote is about not confronting/exposing the perpetrator to a mutual Instagram contact, not explicitly about institutions; the story gives no reason for not going to any institution, hence not_stated. She says she will 'probably' return to counseling and has 'never really talked about it before' (@ 43:34), so no therapy contact about this harm is shown. Perpetrator later admitted the personas were 'a big lie' and apologised (@ 17:54). The ex-husband's corroboration is relayed only through Kaelyn's account.

quotes.quote: so I feel like because of that I repressed a lot of it and it hasn't really come out until talking about it now because I just never talked about it really before.

persons.name: Kaelyn (ex-boyfriend)
persons.harm: After the catfishing, a boyfriend dismissed her grief over 'Tyler' and was, in her words, emotionally abusive, leading her to repress the experience.
persons.outcome_quote: anytime I would talk about Tyler or like cry about him, he would just be like, I don't know why you care, you never met met him or you know he was just very like emotionally abusive
persons.notes: Very brief; told in two sentences. Separate perpetrator from P01, so a separate record per instructions. How the relationship ended is not stated.

persons.name: Tiffany (another person catfished by Kaelyn's friend)
persons.harm: According to Kaelyn (relaying what Tiffany told her), the same perpetrator manipulated Tiffany into believing a little girl had died, and money was sent to a family that did not exist; the perpetrator also told Tiffany that Kaelyn had slept with the perpetrator's husband.
persons.outcome_quote: [perpetrator] had catfished multiple people, and one of them who her name is Tiffany, ended up catfishing her back in order to get revenge, and that was what the whole catfish episode was about.
persons.notes: Second-hand account (Kaelyn relaying Tiffany); Kaelyn hedges ('I might be saying this wrong'). The season says nothing about whether Tiffany went to any institution, so reached_institution is 'unclear' and no contacts are recorded; outcome coded not_protected because no institutional action is shown. MTV took the Catfish episode down, which Kaelyn understood was over the use of children's pictures and fear of legal action (@ 35:12); this is a TV network acting on its own, not a response to Tiffany's harm, so not coded as a contact. Not the host (Tiffany Reese).

contacts.institution: Old Chicago restaurant, downtown Denver (server and bartender)
contacts.when: the same evening, while she was at the bar
contacts.what_was_asked: Nothing; staff acted on their own after recognising the man's pattern.
contacts.what_institution_did: A server followed her into the restroom and warned her the man next to her had lured her there and did this repeatedly; the bartender put her shots in the cooler, staff watched over her, bought her dinner, let her stay for hours and walked her to her car.
contacts.quote: the bartender walked me to my car to make sure that there was nobody out there.
contacts.what_happened_next: The man got angry when she refused him and left; she stayed about four hours and then got home safely.
contacts.notes: Coded as an institution of type 'other' (a business with the power to act on its premises). The warning itself is at s6-e2-predator-jez @ 14:29 ('whatever reason you're here, it's because of him. He got you here.'). The staff said they had no proof and were 'doing the most that they could' (@ 19:39).

contacts.institution: police (department not named; she called a non-emergency line, apparently in the Denver area)
contacts.what_was_asked: To let police know about the man's behaviour because he could be dangerous to other women.
contacts.what_institution_did: Police were polite but said nothing could be done because he was not technically doing anything illegal; they told her to call back if he followed or stalked her.
contacts.quote: I remember they were nice. They were just, they were like, well, there's nothing we can really do about that. They're not technically doing anything illegal.
contacts.what_happened_next: Nothing further. She accepted it ('that was fair'). The man was never identified.
contacts.notes: Police gave a reason (no crime yet), not disbelief, so did_nothing_or_delayed.

persons.decisive_work_quote: I have to talk to you about that guy. And I was like, what guy? Cause I was like, he stood me up. Like I don't, and she's like, no, not that one. The one sitting next to you.
persons.time_to_first_effective_action: the same evening, while the lure was under way
persons.name: Jez
persons.harm: At about 25, a man using a fake Plenty of Fish profile ('Jordan') lured her to an Old Chicago restaurant in Denver, texted excuses while he sat near her as a 'stranger', pressed drinks on her and tried hard to get her to leave with him. Staff told her this was a repeated pattern in which women who were 'stood up' ended up more drunk than expected and left with him.
persons.perpetrator_role: an unidentified man using a fake dating profile
persons.outcome_quote: know who this person is and I don't know what his true intentions were
persons.notes: Outcome partly_protected: restaurant staff kept her safe that night, but police took no action and the man was never identified or stopped, so his pattern could continue. If restaurant staff are not counted as an institution, the outcome would be not_protected (harm stopped by her own refusal; police declined). Crime Junkie later featured the story (Dec 2020) hoping it 'brings awareness and accountability' (s6-e5-massacre-at-the-tree-of-life-synagogue-je @ 1:17); no institutional result is reported. Jez mentions earlier harm by 'a person who was a sociopath' (s6-e2-predator-jez @ 21:40) with no story told, so no separate record.

When she posted about it, another therapist commented that she should do more of her own therapy work (victim blaming, @ 26:38-27:43); that was an individual, not an institution. No report to anyone is mentioned. She mentions a sexual trauma history (bare).

contacts.institution: local police precinct (Pittsburgh, J.E.'s jurisdiction)
contacts.what_was_asked: Protection and an investigation into the threatening antisemitic and homophobic voicemails naming J.E.
contacts.what_institution_did: The officer was caring; a police car was parked outside J.E.'s home around the clock for about a week, and patrols were increased within a few blocks for at least two weeks. The case was passed up to county police and the FBI.
contacts.quote: For the first, at least the first couple of days, maybe slightly under a week there, was actually a police car parked outside for 24 hours.
contacts.what_happened_next: The calls did not stop. The protective detail ended after a week or two.
contacts.notes: In the 2020 episode J.E. says police 'did take it really seriously'; in the 2023-24 update J.E. says 'it was clear to me that local law enforcement didn't take it seriously' and that offices were not versed in antisemitism, homophobia or trans identities (33-wcn-presents-je-s6-updates @ 15:07). Coded acted_partly: real protective steps, but less than needed and they stalled. The victim impact statement read on air (23-wcn-presents-je-s6-updates @ 15:07) confirms the 24-hour detail.

contacts.institution: J.E.'s editor at a remote contract reporting job
contacts.what_was_asked: Time off to speak with police/investigators.
contacts.what_institution_did: J.E. lost the job shortly afterwards; J.E. cannot say for certain that it was because of this.
contacts.quote: I lost my job shortly after I told my then editor I'd have to step away to speak to investigators about what was happening. And even though I related plainly, sapped of emotion or subjectivity, I imagined they thought it was something I must have made up.
contacts.what_happened_next: Lost the contract job.
contacts.notes: J.E. calls it a contract position that 'was already going to be like a temporary gig' (s6-e6-panic-attack-city-je @ 24:01) and says 'I can't say for certain, but I likely lost a contract job' (13-wcn-presents-je-s6-updates @ 17:06). Because the cause is uncertain, coded unclear and not counted as institutional harm.

contacts.institution: Allegheny County police and the FBI (Pittsburgh), with an FBI liaison
contacts.what_institution_did: The case went up to county police and the FBI; an FBI liaison was contacted after each call; J.E. had to give screenshots of an 8chan thread to an older detective and read them aloud to him. The calls came from a rerouted number that could not be traced, and the investigation went dormant.
contacts.quote: The calls didn't stop. They, I mean, the case was immediately sort of like sent up to Allegheny PD, which is like the county PD as well as the FBI.
contacts.what_happened_next: Calls went on for six to eight months, then stopped for a while; by late 2020 the FBI investigation was 'pretty much dormant' (13-wcn-presents-je-s6-updates @ 11:53).
contacts.notes: J.E. found reading the threats aloud to a detective who 'didn't really understand internet stuff' retraumatizing (s6-e6-panic-attack-city-je @ 23:00).

contacts.institution: detectives assigned to the case (local/county)
contacts.when: 2019, during the first wave of calls
contacts.what_institution_did: J.E.'s persistent calls asking for updates were rarely returned.
contacts.quote: I called the detectives assigned to the case with persistence, begging for updates. My calls were rarely returned.
contacts.what_happened_next: No progress until the calls resumed in 2022 and the case moved to the Miami FBI.
contacts.notes: J.E. also says it was 'demoralizing and demeaning to try to have to make my case over and over again to have to explain why something like this was anti-Semitic' (33-wcn-presents-je-s6-updates @ 15:07), which could support 'disbelieved'; the quoted passage most directly shows inaction.

contacts.institution: a therapist (after months on waitlists)
contacts.what_was_asked: Mental health care for the trauma of the calls.
contacts.what_institution_did: At first J.E. could not get care because waitlists were months long and J.E. had no insurance; after months J.E. found a therapist and was able to talk through it.
contacts.quote: I found a therapist after months of waiting, and had space to truly articulate the ways in which I'd been confined in a prison of someone else's making.
contacts.what_happened_next: J.E. began to recover for a time, until the second wave of calls.
contacts.notes: Delay was caused by waitlists and lack of insurance (s6-e6-panic-attack-city-je @ 25:04-26:09, cost_or_access), not by the therapist.

contacts.institution: Anti-Defamation League (ADL), advocacy organisation
contacts.when: before or during the 2022-2023 second wave (timing not stated)
contacts.what_was_asked: To get the FBI to act on the case.
contacts.what_institution_did: After J.E.'s and their mother's legwork, the ADL brought the case to the FBI's attention; ADL staff attended the sentencing.
contacts.quote: At least a couple were from the ADL who were instrumental in elevating this case to the FBI's attention. After all the legwork that I did and my mom did, they really brought it to their attention.
contacts.what_happened_next: The Miami FBI field office took over the investigation.
contacts.notes: Who contacted the ADL first is not stated. J.E. has 'my own thoughts and feelings about the ADL' but credits it.

contacts.institution: FBI Miami field office
contacts.what_institution_did: The agents identified the caller (a woman in California), working from the evidence including the recorded calls, and she was arrested in March 2023. The liaison agent supported J.E. throughout.
contacts.quote: The agents who essentially investigated the case and were able to identify who this caller was were really, really wonderful.
contacts.what_happened_next: She was arrested in March 2023, let out on bond, arrested again for violence against her partner, then extradited to Florida.
contacts.notes: initiated_by third_party = the ADL's escalation; the recordings were made by J.E.'s mother. The FBI told the family little while the investigation was open.

contacts.institution: federal prosecutors (Southern District of Florida)
contacts.what_was_asked: Prosecution, including for a hate crime.
contacts.what_institution_did: Prosecutors charged her, including with a hate crime; she pleaded guilty; at sentencing they played a montage of the worst threats.
contacts.quote: She did plead guilty. The majority of cases that are brought to court, the defendant does plead guilty. There are reasons as to why that happens. There was overwhelming hard forensic evidence that did show that these calls were made from her residence.
contacts.what_happened_next: Sentencing hearing in Miami, with victim impact statements.
contacts.notes: Competency was assessed by both prosecution and defence during discovery (13-wcn-presents-je-s6-updates @ 22:18).

contacts.institution: federal court, Miami (sentencing judge)
contacts.what_was_asked: A fair and just sentence; J.E. gave a victim impact statement.
contacts.what_institution_did: The judge credited J.E.'s statement as showing the calls were premeditated, took account of the homophobia and transphobia, rejected the defence's proposed 12 months and imposed 32 months with three years of supervised release.
contacts.quote: The judge delivered his sentence. In the end, she was given 32 months with time served. So that's a few years with three years of supervised release.
contacts.what_happened_next: She is in a federal facility in California; any contact after release would violate supervised release. J.E. turned down restitution; an appeal was filed but seemingly dropped.
contacts.notes: J.E. asked: 'why had it taken this long for somebody to finally believe and like state out loud something that was so thoroughly clear from the very beginning?' (33-wcn-presents-je-s6-updates @ 10:02).

persons.time_to_first_effective_action: about four years: first police report February 2019; ADL escalation and Miami FBI investigation in 2022-23; arrest March 2023
persons.name: J.E. (the caller)
persons.harm: Months after the Tree of Life massacre, a woman who seems to have found J.E. through their Vanity Fair essay left hundreds of antisemitic, homophobic and transphobic voicemails on J.E.'s stepfather's phones, addressed to J.E. by their first name, threatening to shoot, behead and sexually assault J.E. This happened in two waves (2019, and October 2022 to March 2023), nearly five years in all, and J.E. was also targeted on 8chan.
persons.perpetrator_role: an unknown woman caller ('the Caller'), later identified and convicted
persons.outcome_quote: Meaning that after she's released, if she tries to contact us, she'll be arrested and imprisoned.
persons.notes: Decisive work is hard to call. The mother recorded calls to build forensic evidence, and J.E. and the mother did the 'legwork' that led the ADL to escalate the case to the FBI; the Miami FBI then identified the caller, and the plea rested on 'hundreds of recordings' and forensic evidence. Coded family_or_friends (gathering evidence plus escalation), but the_person and institution are plausible. Whether 'effective action' starts at the ADL escalation or the arrest, it was about four years after the first report; months = Feb 2019 to Mar 2023. The 2019 police detail gave temporary safety and is not counted as effective. Harm stopped with the arrest; J.E. still calls the security 'temporary' because supervised release ends (33-wcn-presents-je-s6-updates @ 19:16). The victim impact statement read on air counts as document_read_on_air; 'court documentation' citing 238 recorded calls is mentioned (13-wcn-presents-je-s6-updates @ 16:01). Journalists covering the sentencing erased J.E. and would not correct errors (33-wcn-presents-je-s6-updates @ 22:19-24:27); media are not treated as institutions here. The perpetrator is a woman of colour with untreated mental illness, per J.E.

persons.name: J.E. (Tree of Life massacre)
persons.harm: A gunman murdered 11 members of J.E.'s synagogue community at Tree of Life, Pittsburgh, on October 27, 2018, people J.E. knew, and J.E.'s parents would normally have been there. J.E. was not present but was left with PTSD and grief.
persons.perpetrator_role: the Tree of Life shooter (antisemitic gunman)
persons.outcome_quote: I couldn't step foot into any synagogue for a really long time. It's still really hard for me to do it.
persons.notes: The harm is the massacre's impact on J.E. as a bereaved community member, not a direct attack, which makes outcome codes a poor fit. No protective or justice outcome (arrest, trial, sentence of the shooter) is mentioned anywhere in the season, so not_protected means only that no institutional protection is shown. The Vanity Fair essay read on air counts as document_read_on_air. A childhood antisemitic slur incident (s6-e5-massacre-at-the-tree-of-life-synagogue-je @ 10:56) is a bare mention.

persons.name: Tiffany Reese (Craigslist room viewing)
persons.harm: At about 21, while desperate for housing, she and her husband viewed a cheap room advertised on Craigslist. During the tour the roughly 70-year-old landlord focused on her, invited her to use his wife's bathtub 'any time', invited them to his monthly swinger parties and suggested a sex-for-rent arrangement like another tenant's.

persons.notes: The host's own story, told with her husband, who was present (second witness). Fear of making the landlord angry is the reason given for lying to him, not for avoiding institutions, so the reason is not_stated. Ad on Craigslist; no report to Craigslist or police mentioned. coder_notes: Season 6 is mostly online and tech harm: catfishing (Kaelyn), a dating-app lure (Jez), an expert episode (Ilyse Kennedy), an influencer roundtable (Ari, Charlie, Jill), the Tree of Life massacre and the stalking of J.E.'s family that followed (two episodes plus three 'WCN Presents [J.E.] S6 Updates' episodes, 1/3-3/3, which are in the season folder and are coded as season content), and the host's Craigslist story. Only J.E.'s stalking story has substantial institutional contact. Judgement calls: (1) Old Chicago restaurant staff coded as an institution of type 'other'. (2) Expert and roundtable guests' harassment coded as person records with low confidence. (3) Only the two Tree of Life victims with individual detail (Cecil and David Rosenthal) have records; the others are in others_mentioned. The season never mentions the shooter's arrest or prosecution. (4) Perpetrators' names (Kaelyn's friend, the Craigslist landlord and his wife) are replaced with [perpetrator] in quotes. Names of non-harmed people (family, staff, witnesses) are not used. (5) The end of s06_04 previews an unrelated 'What Came Next' theater-shooting story, not coded. No unassigned episode continues a season 6 story. Everything was read in full.
